issues.legal_issue: A court may accept an unconditional apology and discharge notices concerning breach of an undertaking when the undertaking is later fulfilled before the relevant event.
material_facts: The respondents undertook through counsel to furnish security within a specified time but did not do so within that time.

After notices issued asking why they should not be punished for breaching the undertaking, the respondents appeared personally, tendered an unconditional apology, and filed an affidavit explaining the delay.
The respondents ultimately furnished security before the announced date of the reauction.
issues.conclusion: The Court accepted the unconditional apology and discharged the notices.
issues.legal_principle: The Court accepted the apology in light of the circumstances explained in the affidavit and the respondents’ eventual compliance before the reauction. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this disposition.

rule.if: contempt_notice_for_breach_of_court_undertaking and undertaking_deadline_missed and later_compliance_before_relevant_event and unconditional_apology

predicates.contempt_notice_for_breach_of_court_unde: A court issued a notice asking a person to show why they should not be punished for breaching an undertaking given to that court.
predicates.undertaking_deadline_missed: The person did not perform the undertaking within the time specified.
predicates.later_compliance_before_relevant_event: The person performed the undertaking before the event for which performance was required.
predicates.unconditional_apology: The person appeared before the court and offered an apology without conditions.

issues.definition: When a person misses the deadline for a court undertaking but fulfils it before the relevant event and offers an unconditional apology in response to a contempt notice, the notice is discharged after the apology is accepted.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court, acting as an appellate court, cannot exercise a general supervisory power to call for lower-court records and quash orders on its own motion.
material_facts: The Supreme Court had directed that a reauction be held within a specified period.
A later application in a separate writ proceeding led a High Court judge to stay the reauction on the day it was scheduled.

The separate writ proceeding and the resulting stay order were not before the Supreme Court in an appeal; the Court stated that it had no power to call for the records and quash the order on its own motion.
The Supreme Court expressed serious displeasure at the stay’s effect on its direction but did not quash the stay order.
issues.conclusion: The Court stated that its appellate jurisdiction did not give it supervisory power to call for the lower court’s records and quash the order on its own motion.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished its plenary appellate powers, referred to in connection with Article 136 of the Constitution, from a general power of superintendence. It stated that it was not a court of superintendence and had no power to call for lower-court records and quash orders on its own motion. No earlier case was cited for this proposition.

predicates.supreme_court_appellate_proceeding: The matter before the Supreme Court arises in its appellate capacity.
predicates.lower_court_order_outside_pending_appeal: A lower court made an order in a separate proceeding that is not part of the appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.order_not_brought_before_court_for_appel: The lower-court order has not been brought before the Supreme Court for appellate review.

issues.definition: When the Supreme Court is acting in an appellate matter and a lower-court order from a separate proceeding has not been brought before it for appellate review, it has no general supervisory power to quash that order on its own motion.
